title: Proximity-Induced Targeted Degradation of Microtubule-Associated Protein Tau Pre-mRNA Using Small Bifunctional Molecules.
abstract: Dysregulation of RNA processing caused by single-nucleotide mutations can profoundly alter cellular homeostasis and drive disease. A prominent example is the aberrant alternative splicing of the microtubule-associated protein tau (MAPT) gene, which leads to imbalances in 3R and 4R tau isoforms and is associated with multiple tauopathies. In particular, mutations such as the disinhibition-dementia-parkinsonism-amyotrophy complex (DDPAC) variant promote exon 10 inclusion, increasing the 4R/3R ratio and contributing to tau aggregation and neurodegeneration. Antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) can reduce MAPT mRNA levels, while small molecules have been developed to modulate MAPT pre-mRNA splicing by targeting regulatory RNA structures. Here, we investigated an alternative approach based on Proximity-Induced Nucleic Acid Degradation (PINAD), in which an RNA-binding ligand is conjugated to an RNA-cleaving warhead. We designed and synthesized a library of 24 bifunctional small molecules derived from a previously reported MAPT pre-mRNA SRE-binding ligand. Screening in SH-SY5Y cells identified PINAD-23, which reduced MAPT mRNA levels in a dose-dependent manner and decreased the expression of both 3R and 4R tau isoforms. Biochemical studies using a model MAPT RNA showed that PINAD-23 binds the target RNA and promotes RNA cleavage. Defined cleavage products detected under metal-free conditions supported a contribution from a base-mediated pathway, while Cu(II) binding by the diimidazole warhead and Cu(II)-dependent RNA cleavage supported the involvement of a copper-dependent pathway. These findings provide a proof of concept for converting a previously characterized MAPT RNA-binding ligand into a bifunctional small molecule capable of inducing target RNA cleavage and reducing downstream tau expression.

title: MIsoTEx: a mammalian transcript-isoform classification framework and database for exploring tissue distribution, expression stability, and abundance patterns.
abstract: Alternative splicing generates transcript isoforms with distinct tissue-expression patterns, but resources integrating transcript distribution, abundance consistency, and relative abundance remain limited. We developed MIsoTEx (Mammalian Isoform Tissue Expression Resource), a database and expression-pattern-based classification framework for protein-coding iso-mRNAs in human, mouse, and rat. RNA-seq datasets from GTEx, ARCHS4, and newly curated datasets from SRA were used to construct catalogs, following stringent selection of normal adult tissue samples. Ubiquitously detected iso-mRNAs were classified as uniformly abundant (UUni) or variably abundant (UVar), while tissue-associated iso-mRNAs were classified as tissue-predominant (TPred), tissue-exclusive (TExcl), tissue-poor (TPoor), or tissue-absent (TAbsn). These classes were further divided into five relative-abundance sub-classes, with confidence scores assigned to tissue-associated classifications. MIsoTEx contains ~147 000 protein-coding iso-mRNAs and supports gene- and transcript-based queries, tissue-pattern searches, cross-species comparison of orthologs with concordant expression, and analysis of user-supplied expression data to identify candidate control iso-mRNAs. Comparisons with independent RNA-seq, RT-PCR, and published expression datasets provided support for aspects of the classification framework. Functional enrichment analysis revealed distinct biological associations among selected expression-based categories. MIsoTEx facilitates transcript-level exploration of mammalian tissue-expression patterns and helps identify candidate reference iso-mRNAs for experimental evaluation. The database can be accessed using the link: https://resources.ibab.ac.in/MIsoTEx/.

title: Histone H3K9 lactylation promotes hepatocellular carcinoma progression by activating LUC7L2 to mediate SPINK13 mRNA degradation : A metabolic-epigenetic mechanism linking histone lactylation to RNA destabilization in HCC.
abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is one of the leading causes of cancer-related mortality worldwide, yet the contribution of histone lactylation to its progression remains unclear. Histone H3K9 lactylation (H3K9la) has recently emerged as a metabolic-epigenetic mark linking glycolytic reprogramming to transcriptional regulation. We integrated histone modification profiling, transcriptome assays, RNA-protein interaction analyses, and in vitro and in vivo functional experiments to investigate the role of H3K9la in HCC. Molecular and cellular assays included qPCR, Western blotting, ChIP-qPCR, RIP, RNA stability analysis, and functional rescue. Xenograft mouse models were used to validate mechanistic findings. H3K9la levels were elevated in HCC tissues and cell lines and positively correlated with expression of the RNA-binding protein LUC7L2. Inhibition of glycolysis or lactylation suppressed LUC7L2 expression and reduced tumor cell proliferation, migration, and invasion, while promoting apoptosis. Mechanistically, H3K9la activated LUC7L2 transcription, which in turn bound to and destabilized SPINK13 pre-mRNA, repressing its tumor-suppressive function. Overexpression of SPINK13 inhibited HCC cell growth by inducing G1-phase arrest and reducing AKT phosphorylation, whereas its knockdown rescued the inhibitory effects of LUC7L2 silencing. In vivo, blockade of lactylation suppressed tumor growth and downregulated LUC7L2, an effect reversed by SPINK13 silencing or LUC7L2 overexpression. Our findings establish a novel H3K9la-LUC7L2-SPINK13 regulatory axis that links lactate metabolism to post-transcriptional gene silencing and malignant progression in HCC. Targeting this pathway provides a promising epigenetic-metabolic therapeutic strategy.

title: Structural and biochemical insights into infectious bronchitis virus endoribonuclease Nsp15.
abstract: RNA viruses are not only a human health concern but also an economic concern due to animal infections in major industries. Nsp15, a uridine-specific endoribonuclease conserved across vertebrate nidoviruses, processes viral RNA to evade detection by the host immune system. While the enzymatic function is conserved, the oligomeric state necessary for activity does not appear to be strictly conserved across nidoviruses. How oligomerization affects Nsp15 RNA recognition and processing remains understudied. Here, we report the first cryogenic electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) structure of a γ-coronavirus Nsp15, using infectious bronchitis virus (IBV), a major poultry pathogen, as a model γ-coronavirus. The structure was determined at 2.4 Å resolution and reveals that IBV Nsp15 adopts the characteristic hexameric architecture observed in α- and β-coronavirus Nsp15, including HCoV-229E, SARS-CoV-2, SARS-CoV, MERS-CoV, and MHV. To investigate IBV Nsp15 substrate specificity, we performed endoribonuclease assays using diverse RNA substrates. Despite the high degree of conserved structure, we used Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) to show that IBV Nsp15 exhibits distinct substrate preferences for the nucleotide adjacent to the cleavage site, though this preference does appear to be context-dependent when using more complicated substrates. We also demonstrate that, while not essential for catalysis, divalent metal ions enhance endoribonuclease activity. Collectively, these findings establish the structural and functional framework for γ-coronavirus Nsp15 activity, uncover differences in RNA substrate specificity, and highlight conserved and divergent features of Nsp15 across different nidoviruses that could be utilized for the development of new antiviral targets.IMPORTANCEInfectious bronchitis virus (IBV), a γ-coronavirus, is a major poultry pathogen that encodes an endoribonuclease conserved across coronaviruses. While its enzymatic function is conserved, assembly differs across the viral family. Structural studies revealed that the IBV endoribonuclease assembles into a hexameric structure much like other coronaviruses, yet Förster resonance energy transfer assays demonstrated a sequence preference for the nucleotide 5' to the cleaved base that has not been observed with previous homologs. Additionally, we found that metal ions can boost endoribonuclease activity but are not strictly required. These findings establish a structural and biochemical framework of the IBV endoribonuclease and expand our knowledge of the enzyme across coronaviruses.

title: [Berberine targets Smurf2 to regulate the TGF-β/Smads signaling pathway and alleviate myocardial fibrosis in rats with atrial fibrillation].
abstract: Objective: To explore the therapeutic efficacy and related mechanism of berberine in treating atrial fibrillation by regulating the transforming growth factor β (TGF-β)/Smads signaling pathway. Methods: The SD rats were divided into the normal group, the model group, the low-dose berberine group, the medium-dose berberine group, the high-dose berberine group, the amiodarone group, and the SRI-011381 group (SRI-011381 is a TGF-β signaling pathway activator). The atrial fibrillation rat model was constructed by injecting acetylcholine and calcium chloride. The fibrotic model was constructed by stimulating primary atrial fibroblasts with angiotensin Ⅱ (AngⅡ). The cells were divided into the control group, the AngⅡ group, the low berberine group, the high berberine group, the berberine+si-NC group (si-NC was a negative control small interfering RNA), and the berberine+si-Smad ubiquitination regulatory factor 2 (Smurf2) group (si-Smurf2 was a small interfering RNA targeting Smurf2). The pathological changes of atrial tissue were detected by hematoxylin-eosin staining, the fibrosis of atrial tissue was examined by Masson staining, and the expression levels of α-smooth muscle actin (α-SMA), type Ⅰ collagen, type Ⅲ collagen, Smurf2, TGF-β1, p-Smad3, p-Smad2, Smad7, and TGF-β receptor type Ⅰ (TβR-Ⅰ) were detected by Western blotting. The pull-down experiment was used to screen the target proteins related to berberine. The relevant target proteins were then subjected to KEGG pathway enrichment analysis. Molecular docking was performed using AutoDock. Results: In rats, compared with the normal group, the duration of atrial fibrillation in the model group was increased, and the pathological damage and fibrosis of the atrial tissue were aggravated (P<0.05); compared with the model group, the high-dose berberine group showed a reduction in the duration of atrial fibrillation after treatment, and the pathological damage and fibrosis of the atrial tissue were alleviated (P<0.05). The pull-down experiment identified Smurf2 as the key target for the treatment of atrial fibrillation with berberine; KEGG analysis revealed that the key pathway was the TGF-β signaling pathway; molecular docking showed that berberine had a strong binding affinity for Smurf2. In the cells, compared with the AngⅡ group, the expression levels of TGF-β1, p-Smad3, p-Smad2, TβR-Ⅰ, type Ⅰ collagen, type Ⅲ collagen, and α-SMA proteins in the the low-dose berberine group, high-dose berberine group and the berberine+si-NC group were decreased, while the expression levels of Smurf2 and Smad7 proteins were increased (P<0.05); compared with the berberine+si-NC group, the expression levels of TGF-β1, p-Smad3, p-Smad2, TβR-Ⅰ, type Ⅰ collagen, type Ⅲ collagen, and α-SMA proteins in the berberine+si-Smurf2 group were increased, while the expression levels of Smurf2 and Smad7 proteins were decreased (P<0.05). In rats, compared with the model group, the expression levels of TGF-β1, p-Smad3, p-Smad2, TβR-Ⅰ, type Ⅰ collagen, type Ⅲ collagen, and α-SMA proteins in the high-dose berberine group were decreased, while the expression level of Smad7 protein was increased (P<0.05); compared with the high-dose berberine group, the expression levels of TGF-β1, p-Smad3, p-Smad2, TβR-Ⅰ, type Ⅰ collagen, type Ⅲ collagen, and α-SMA proteins in the SRI-011381 group were increased, while the expression level of Smad7 protein was decreased (P<0.05). Conclusion: Berberine may alleviate myocardial fibrosis in atrial fibrillation rats by targeting Smurf2 to inhibit the TGF-β/Smads signaling pathway.

title: Revisiting Holley's Alternative tRNA Structures: Roles for His Non-Cloverleaf Conformations.
abstract: Transfer RNAs (tRNA) are an integral component of protein synthesis, where they facilitate the transfer of amino acids to the growing peptide chain via recognition of codons on the messenger RNA (mRNA). The primary structure of tRNA was first worked out by Robert Holley and coworkers in 1965, for which Holley was awarded the Nobel Prize. In that report, they offered several secondary structure models for tRNA: one was the now well-known cloverleaf conformation, but others were rod-shaped and multi-helical. Recent developments in tRNA structure probing via tRNA structure-seq have provided the means to derive tRNA conformations in vivo. This has led to mounting evidence for the presence of alternative structures of tRNA in the cell including rod-shaped and multi-helical ones, the populations of which can vary with external stimuli such as heat stress. In this Perspective, we revisit Holley's seminal contributions in light of recent experimental approaches for probing tRNA structure in the cell. While early in vitro studies clearly identified alternative tRNA conformations, we provide evidence for alternative conformations of tRNA in vivo, as proposed by Holley over 60 years ago. When possible, we separate alternative tRNA structures into partially folded, misfolded, and remodeled forms, which have the potential to be either detrimental or productive to cellular function. We conclude by considering biological implications of alternative tRNA conformations in cells and the prospects for additional contributions of altered tRNA structures to cellular function.

title: Certified Comparative Statics for Conservation-Law Equilibrium Layers, with an Application to RNA Interference
abstract: Implicit and equilibrium neural layers define their output as the fixed point of a map. Existing theory certifies that this fixed point exists; it does not certify how it responds to its inputs. For a conservation-law layer with order-preserving coupling we give a form-independent answer: every input-output comparative static is sign-certified if and only if the residual Jacobian is a nonsingular M-matrix, and the certified sign depends only on the sign of the occupancy derivative, so one guarantee covers Langmuir, Hill, and saturating-exponential occupancies. The M-matrix machinery is classical; the contribution is form-independence as the portable invariant, the first certified-sign sensitivity result for a layer of this class, and a sharp phase boundary at which certification is lost while the equilibrium remains well posed. Three consequences follow: the phase boundary, which is strictly stronger than the M-matrix condition; competitive derepression, whose derivative is identically zero for any independent per-target scorer and provably nonzero here; and non-submodularity of resource-coupled suppression. We instantiate on siRNA off-target competition and validate on real public data only, across seventeen microRNAs, two titration studies, and a paired chemical-modification experiment; a second, non-biological instantiation shows the same certified sign on measured physical data. As a trainable layer the operator learns end-to-end while remaining certified-monotone by construction, reaching magnitude parity with a parameter-matched feedforward baseline while expressing a competition effect that baseline cannot represent for any weights. The single-pool instantiation validates the mechanism but does not rank off-target magnitude or resolve position-specific design. Code: https://github.com/shadi97kh/certified-equilibrium-layers

title: Familial VAMP2-Related Disorder With Generalized Epilepsy Caused by an Intronic Regulatory Variant With Evidence of Haploinsufficiency.
abstract: Pathogenic variants in VAMP2, encoding the synaptic vesicle SNARE protein synaptobrevin-2, cause a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by intellectual disability, autism, epilepsy, and movement disorders. Reported variants are predominantly de novo missense changes affecting the SNARE motif; loss-of-function variants are associated with haploinsufficiency, causing milder phenotypes. We describe a proband and his mother carrying a heterozygous intronic VAMP2 variant (NM_014232.3:c.2+4A>G) identified by exome sequencing. We performed clinical and functional RNA analyses to investigate pathogenicity. The proband's phenotype included moderate intellectual disability, autism spectrum disorder, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, and valproate-responsive childhood absence epilepsy. The affected mother had juvenile absence epilepsy, intellectual disability, and bipolar disorder. Quantitative RNA analysis demonstrated reduced VAMP2 expression in both affected individuals, supporting a loss-of-function mechanism consistent with haploinsufficiency. Our findings expand the genetic and inheritance spectrum of VAMP2-related disorders by demonstrating a familial syndrome caused by a regulatory intronic variant associated with reduced gene expression.

title: RNA-Guided Genome Organization Across Scales.
abstract: The genome is hierarchically folded, from one-dimensional organization along the chromatin fiber involving nucleosomes, epigenetic marks, and proteins to three-dimensional regulatory element-driven chromatin loops and large chromatin domains. These layers are spatially coordinated with nuclear bodies to shape genome organization in a spatiotemporal manner. Genome folding is not a static architectural outcome but rather an actively regulated process requiring the coordinated action of diverse molecular factors across scales. Although DNA sequence, histone modifications, and proteins have traditionally been viewed as the primary determinants of genome organization, RNA has recently emerged as an integral regulatory layer shaping genome architecture. Beyond serving as a transcriptional output, RNA functions as an active organizational component that modulates chromatin structure, stabilizes regulatory interactions, and coordinates molecular assemblies within the nucleus. In this review, we present a conceptual framework for RNA-mediated genome organization across scales, emphasizing unifying principles rather than individual molecular players or RNA classes while drawing on selected well-studied examples for illustration.

title: Transcript Direct Repair: RNA-Guided Pathways of DNA Double-Strand Break Repair.
abstract: The Central Dogma of molecular biology has traditionally emphasized a unidirectional flow of genetic information from DNA to RNA to protein, with RNA-to-DNA information transfer being viewed as a specialized process associated primarily with selfish genetic elements or telomere maintenance. However, emerging evidence demonstrates that endogenous RNA directly participates in DNA double-strand break (DSB) repair. We synthesize these findings within the framework of transcript direct repair (TDR), defining pathways in which transcripts serve as genetic templates or structural scaffolds to facilitate repair. We highlight how eukaryotic DNA polymerases, including Pol θ and Pol ζ, utilize intrinsic reverse transcriptase activity for RNA-templated DNA synthesis independent of viral enzymes. By unifying RNA-templated homologous recombination and RNA-mediated end-joining mechanisms, we establish TDR as a crucial, physiological component of genome maintenance. Finally, we discuss TDR's evolutionary implications, such as whole-intron deletions, illustrating how endogenous transcription shapes long-term genome remodeling.

title: Architecture of the poxvirus early-transcription machinery and portal complex.
abstract: Poxviruses enclose a complete viral transcription machinery alongside their dsDNA genome within the viral core, a transcription-competent compartment delimited by a permeable multi-layered protein shell. Upon infection of a cell and core release, this machinery almost immediately starts synthesizing early mRNAs, which are extruded across the core wall into the cytoplasm for translation. While in vitro structures of the isolated viral DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (vRNAP) have been described1-3, its native in virio architecture, spatial organization, and physical coupling to the genome remain unknown. Using cryo-electron tomography and sub-tomogram averaging on purified Vaccinia virus cores, we reveal that packaged vRNAP exists not as monomer, but as massive 1.8 MDa resting-state dimer bridged by fully ordered vaccinia virus early transcription factor (VETF). We also identify a subpopulation of these dimers bound to the essential kinase VPK2 and the core protein L4, which directly tether the transcribing engines to the packaged genome near the inner core wall. Furthermore, we determine a sub-nanometer structure of the putative poxvirus mRNA extrusion portal complex, revealing a rigid assembly integrated into the core wall comprising an E8 hexameric crown, an E6 hexameric central hub, and a basal L3 dodecameric channel suited for nucleic acid export. Together, these structures provide a comprehensive architectural blueprint of important components of the poxvirus core and open new structural and functional avenues for investigating poxvirus genome packaging, transcription activation, and mRNA extrusion.

title: Metal ion-assisted separation of nucleic acids with different topologies.
abstract: Metal ions are added to DNA or RNA solutions to enhance the efficiency of many molecular biology procedures, but information about their utility for structure-selective separation of nucleic acid isoforms is limited. In this study we show that heat denaturation of linear DNA or RNA in the presence of divalent cations, followed by rapid cooling, promotes formation of insoluble high-molecular-weight aggregates that can be detected by gel electrophoresis and light scattering and removed by microcentrifugation. Calcium ions worked effectively at low concentrations (< 10 mM), while other divalent metals such as Mg2+, Sr2+ and Ba2+ required higher concentrations. Monovalent lithium, sodium and potassium ions were ineffective under the conditions tested. Unaggregated isoforms were readily recovered from supernatants, but retrieval from pelleted Ca-DNA aggregates required incubation at elevated temperatures. DNAs could also be precipitated by Ca2+ ions after denaturation with formamide or DMSO. RNA oligonucleotides, but not DNA oligonucleotides, were selectively removed from aqueous solutions, though higher calcium concentrations were required. Interestingly, circular plasmid DNAs were resistant to calcium-induced aggregate formation and could be separated from linear DNAs by a mechanism that depended primarily on structure rather than size. The results suggest that the strands of the supercoiled plasmids were denatured but topology-constrained, and they rapidly reannealed to form aggregation-resistant double-stranded DNA. This simple metal ion-assisted, structure-selective fractionation of nucleic acid isoforms enables both analytical and preparative enrichment of circular plasmid DNAs from complex mixtures.

title: Diterpenoids From Juniperus squamata With Anti-ZIKV Activity.
abstract: Two new abietane diterpenoids (1-2) and one new labdane diterpenoid (3), named juniuamatades A-C, together with twelve known compounds (4-15), were isolated from Juniperus squamata. The chemical structures of 1-3 were elucidated by comprehensive spectroscopic analysis (1D/2D NMR, HR-ESI-MS, UV, IR, ECD), while the known compounds were identified by the comparison of their NMR spectral data with existing literature data. The biological activity of a subset of the isolated compounds was evaluated. Among the tested isolates, compounds 4 and 6 reduced ZIKV RNA levels and envelope protein expression in a concentration-dependent manner, with half-maximal effective concentrations (EC50) of 9.47 µM and 20.94 µM, respectively.

title: The mechanosensitive channel MscS links lipoteichoic acid synthesis alterations to beta-lactam sensitivity in Staphylococcus aureus.
abstract: Lipoteichoic acid (LTA) is an essential cell envelope polymer in Staphylococcus aureus and contributes to beta-lactam resistance in methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA). Mutations that alter LTA synthesis sensitize MRSA to beta-lactam antibiotics, but the mechanism connecting the envelope polymer defects to antibiotic susceptibility has remained unclear. Here, using suppressor mutants with a mutation in RNA polymerase subunits, we found that LTA synthesis defects increased expression of a ParB-like protein and the mechanosensitive channel MscS. This locus was repressed in RNA polymerase suppressor mutants, which restored beta-lactam resistance, whereas induced expression of both genes reduced resistance. Increased ParBL-MscS expression was associated with decreased intracellular potassium and reduced cyclic di-AMP (c-di-AMP), linking altered membrane-envelope physiology to second messenger signaling. LTA synthesis mutants also showed reduced production of penicillin-binding protein 4 (PBP4), an important determinant of beta-lactam resistance. Modest restoration of PBP4 improved resistance in the mutant with reduced LTA abundance, whereas the mutant producing elongated LTA showed a distinct response, indicating that different LTA defects impose different envelope stresses. Also, under reduced LTA conditions, increased c-di-AMP level alone was not sufficient to restore PBP4 expression and beta-lactam resistance. Together, these findings identify a potassium-dependent pathway connecting LTA synthesis, mechanosensitive channel activity, c-di-AMP signaling, PBP4 production, and beta-lactam resistance. This work reveals how cell envelope perturbations are converted into cytoplasmic regulatory responses that control antibiotic susceptibility and suggests that ion homeostasis and c-di-AMP signaling may be exploitable pathways for restoring beta-lactam efficacy against MRSA.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant S. aureus (MRSA), is difficult to treat because it can withstand many beta-lactam antibiotics. Changes in lipoteichoic acid (LTA), a major cell-envelope polymer, increase beta-lactam sensitivity, but the underlying mechanism has been unclear. Here, we show that LTA synthesis defects activate a pathway involving the predicted membrane channel MscS. This pathway lowers intracellular potassium, reduces cyclic di-AMP signaling, and decreases production of PBP4, a cell-wall synthesis enzyme that contributes to beta-lactam resistance. These changes make MRSA more vulnerable to beta-lactam antibiotics. Our findings show that antibiotic resistance depends not only on drug targets but also on coordination between the cell envelope, ion homeostasis, and intracellular signaling. This connection identifies physiological pathways that may be exploited to restore beta-lactam efficacy against resistant S. aureus.

title: Dual-Handle Purification for Structurally Defined Cap2 mRNA Using Hydrophobic Tag-Assisted Cap Chromatography and Oligo(dT) Affinity Chromatography.
abstract: The application of mRNA-based medicines, such as SARS-CoV-2 vaccines, has expanded to gene therapy and therapeutic protein delivery. RNA products by in vitro transcription (IVT) are intrinsically heterogeneous, comprising short, long, and incompletely processed transcripts. Because the 5' cap and 3' poly(A) tail act synergistically to support intracellular mRNA stability and efficient translation, preserving structural integrity across the entire transcript is a critical quality attribute for therapeutic mRNA manufacturing. Therefore, we established an integrated production workflow for producing structurally defined Cap2 mRNA while preserving structural integrity across the entire transcript. A 4.1-kb mRNA model is transcribed using a hydrophobic-tagged Cap2 analog. Ion-pair reversed-phase HPLC enriches the tagged Cap2 transcripts and purges any uncapped species and dsRNA impurities. An intermediate in-line UV-A photocleavage process is applied to photodecage and restore cap structure. Subsequent oligo(dT) affinity chromatography selectively isolates poly(A)-containing transcripts, enabling sequential enrichment of both terminal structural elements: the 5' cap and 3' poly(A) tail. The final product consisted almost entirely of capped transcripts, exhibited enhanced size uniformity, and contained dsRNA below the detection limit of the dot-blot assay. Spike protein expression was demonstrated, supporting the proposed production workflow as an effective strategy for generating structurally defined Cap2 mRNA.

title: miRTarBase 11.0: an evidence-centred resource for experimentally supported microRNA-target interactions.
abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression through sequence-dependent interactions with target RNAs, but different experimental approaches capture distinct aspects of miRNA-target interactions (MTIs). miRTarBase 11.0 contains 9771 947 MTI records derived from literature curation, integrated CLASHub chimeric-pairing data and processed Argonaute cross-linking and immunoprecipitation (AGO-CLIP) data, encompassing 5010 miRNAs and 31 539 target genes. To support interaction-level interpretation, the resource distinguishes direct pairing evidence, AGO occupancy, functional validation, and contextual support. Integration of CLASHub provides binding-site-resolved evidence of direct miRNA-target pairing, while updated AGO CLIP processing defines high-confidence and conserved interaction classes. A rule-based score summarises annotated targeting or binding methods, protein- and RNA-related assays, rescue experiments, and functional assays, while complementary tiers distinguish method combinations. RNA2Immune places MTIs in immune-cell and disease contexts; Rfam 15.0 and miRBase v23 provide harmonized miRNA family, sequence, and identifier annotations; and NPInter v5.0 links upstream noncoding RNA regulators to miRNA-target networks. A Qwen3.6-27B-assisted workflow supports full-text and figure-based curation with human verification. The redesigned Django and Nginx platform supports secure operation, stable deployment and responsive access to evidence-ranked searches, contextual browsing, network views, and data downloads. miRTarBase 11.0 is freely available without registration at https://awi.cuhk.edu.cn/miRTarBase/.

title: Newcastle disease virus is a safe and immunogenic respiratory-delivered vaccine against SARS-CoV-2 in a ferret model.
abstract: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) has caused close to 800 million infections and over 7 million deaths worldwide. In addition to its impact on human health, the virus has shown cross-species transmission, including spillover into mustelids such as mink. Here, we evaluated the safety, immunogenicity, and efficacy of a live attenuated Newcastle disease virus (NDV) vaccine expressing a prefusion-stabilized (PFS) SARS-CoV-2 spike protein (pS), delivered intranasally in domestic ferrets, included in the study as a well-established model of upper respiratory infection in humans, and a representative mustelid species. The vaccine (NDV-PFS) was safe and immunogenic, promoting a systemic antibody response and plasma neutralizing activity against the Ancestral, Delta, and, to a lesser degree, Omicron variant. Upon intranasal challenge with the Ancestral strain, vaccination conferred protection against virus replication, reducing SARS-CoV-2 RNA in the nasal turbinates by approximately five orders of magnitude, and eliminating detectable virus antigen in turbinates by immunohistochemistry. Importantly, both single- and double-dose regimens reduced SARS-CoV-2 replication to a similar extent, indicating that this vaccine platform may be amenable to single-dose administration. Overall, NDV-PFS proved to be a safe, immunogenic, and protective intranasal vaccine against SARS-CoV-2 in ferrets. As the first study to evaluate an NDV-vectored vaccine in this species, this study expands the range of animals in which this platform has proven effective, and supports further development of NDV-based mucosal vaccines for respiratory pathogens in multiple species.

title: Inhaled Nanomedicines for Pulmonary Fibrosis: Linking Pulmonary Barriers to Formulation Design and Translational Evaluation.
abstract: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is characterized by excessive extracellular matrix deposition and disruption of alveolar architecture, leading to impaired lung function. Pirfenidone and nintedanib can slow lung function decline in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, but do not reverse established fibrosis, and adverse effects may limit continued treatment. Inhaled nanomedicines offer opportunities to improve pulmonary drug exposure through coordinated formulation and device design. This review briefly outlines pathological features relevant to delivery and examines how fibrosis modifies aerosol access, mucus transport, macrophage interactions and interstitial penetration. It distinguishes aerosol aerodynamic size from nanocarrier size and discusses design trade-offs involving surface charge, hydrophilicity and carrier mechanics in relation to target cells and disease context. Platforms are organized into polymeric systems, lipid-based systems, naturally derived extracellular vesicles, protein- and nucleic-acid-based assemblies, drug-based dispersions and powders, and carbon-based and coordination-framework systems. Nano-in-micro formulations are considered separately as an architecture connecting aerosol deposition with subsequent nanocarrier release. Selected micrometer-scale formulations provide comparative context for aerosol design. Representative studies are evaluated for delivery performance, therapeutic outcomes, safety and biodistribution, alongside advances in RNA delivery and combination strategies. Recent clinical developments in inhaled PF therapies are discussed separately from evidence for nanocarrier-based formulations. Evidence for most nanomedicine platforms remains preclinical. Further translation requires quantitative regional exposure measurements, functional delivery to intended cells, disease-relevant models, reproducible formulation-device performance and repeated-dose pulmonary safety.

title: Regioselective esterification of ginsenoside Rg1 yields anti-DENV derivatives with reduced viral NS3 expression.
abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) poses a major global health burden, and clinically approved antiviral drugs remain scarce. Leveraging a regioselective esterification strategy of ginsenoside Rg1, we synthesized nineteen derivatives (I1-I19) and evaluated their anti-DENV-2 activity using the New Guinea C strain. Among them, I6 and I17 reduced extracellular DENV RNA levels in Vero cells, with the responses approaching a non-zero plateau at higher concentrations, with EC50 values of 17.77 ± 2.79 μM and 5.50 ± 0.70 μM (ribavirin, the assay control: 98.35 ± 5.84 μM). The compounds also showed low cytotoxicity, with CC50 > 400 μM. Western blotting and immunofluorescence assays demonstrated that both compounds reduced DENV NS3 protein expression in infected cells. These results identify I6 and I17 as promising Rg1-derived anti-DENV candidates and provide a foundation for further optimization of natural-product-derived antiviral scaffolds.

title: Squalenoyl siRNA nanoparticles biodistribution enable non-invasive gene silencing in the central nervous system via intravenous and intranasal delivery.
abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) remains a major obstacle to the delivery of small interfering RNAs (siRNAs) to the central nervous system (CNS), limiting the development of RNA-based therapies for neurological disorders. Squalenoyl nanoparticles (SQ NPs) represent a promising delivery platform due to their self-assembling properties and ability to protect nucleic acids. Here, we evaluated the ability of siRNA-SQ nanoparticles to achieve functional gene silencing in the CNS following intravenous (IV) and intranasal (IN) administration in the PLP-eGFP reporter mouse model. We observed significant reductions in GFP mRNA and protein levels across multiple brain regions and the spinal cord, indicating that the delivered siRNA retained biological activity in the CNS. Pharmacokinetic analyses revealed rapid brain-associated siRNA exposure (Tmax ≈ 5 min), followed by a marked decline and a slower terminal phase (apparent half-life ≈ 80 h) after IV administration. Additionally, systemic administration in two non-human primates (NHPs) resulted in measurable brain-associated antisense siRNA signals, with regional and interindividual variability. These findings suggest that SQ NPs enable functional siRNA delivery to the CNS via both IV and IN routes. The observed mRNA and protein-level silencing supports the potential of this platform for RNA-based therapies targeting neurological disorders, though further studies are needed to elucidate the mechanisms of delivery and optimize translational applications.

title: 2,3-Dimethyldioxy-9-methyl-11-methoxy-8,10-azacyclo berberine chloride promotes TNFRSF19-mediated endoplasmic reticulum stress to induce paraptosis in non-small cell lung cancer cells.
abstract: Paraptosis, a caspase-independent form of programmed cell death characterized by endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondrial swelling, represents a promising strategy to circumvent apoptosis resistance in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here, we demonstrate that a novel berberine derivative BN-7 induces potent paraptosis in NSCLC cells. BN-7-treated cells exhibited hallmark paraptotic ultrastructural features including marked endoplasmic reticulum (ER) lumen dilation, swollen mitochondria with disrupted cristae, and extensive cytoplasmic vacuolization, accompanied by progressive downregulation of ALG-2-interacting protein X (ALIX) and upregulation of C/EBP homologous protein (CHOP). Flow cytometry demonstrated that BN-7 treatment induced significant accumulation of intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and Ca2+ in a time- and concentration-dependent manner. Immunofluorescence staining revealed pronounced ER network expansion and dilation. Western blot analysis further showed time- and concentration-dependent upregulation of PKR-like endoplasmic reticulum kinase (PERK), immunoglobulin heavy chain-binding protein (BiP), and activating transcription factor 4 (ATF4). RNA sequencing and molecular docking identified tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily member 19 (TNFRSF19) as a candidate binding target of BN-7. Mechanistically, BN-7 upregulated TNFRSF19, which functioned as a critical upstream regulator to amplify ER stress through activation of the PERK-ATF4-CHOP signaling axis. TNFRSF19 knockdown attenuated BN-7-induced ER stress signaling, whereas TNFRSF19 overexpression enhanced ER stress marker induction. In xenograft models, BN-7 dose-dependently suppressed tumor growth with the high-dose regimen achieving efficacy comparable to gemcitabine. These findings identify TNFRSF19 as a key upstream regulator of NSCLC paraptosis and establish BN-7 as a promising paraptosis-inducing agent for overcoming apoptosis-resistant lung cancer.

title: Thalamocortical vulnerability in autism spectrum disorder: a computational model of CPEB4 mis-splicing.
abstract: Skipping of a neuronal microexon in cytoplasmic polyadenylation element-binding protein 4 (CPEB4) transcripts has been linked to idiopathic autism spectrum disorder, but the most susceptible brain regions and cell types are unknown. We asked whether the balance between the splicing activator serine/arginine repetitive matrix 4 (SRRM4) and the RNA-binding repressors polypyrimidine tract-binding proteins 1 and 2 (PTBP1 and PTBP2) is sufficient to predict regional differences in microexon inclusion, and which predictions withstand uncertainty in unmeasured parameters. We modeled their competitive binding to the intronic motifs flanking the microexon, including destabilization of SRRM4 expression by sustained histone deacetylase inhibition, and applied the model to human brain transcriptomic data from tissue samples, single cells and developmental stages. The thalamus expressed markedly less SRRM4 mRNA than the anterior cingulate cortex, and the model predicted lower microexon inclusion in the thalamus in every draw of the sensitivity analysis, although the size of the difference varied widely and absolute inclusion values were poorly constrained. A larger thalamic effect of histone deacetylase inhibition was not robust: it followed from the assumed regional difference in super-enhancer susceptibility, and the cingulate cortex lost more inclusion when this susceptibility was equal in both regions. The model is not experimentally validated, and microexon inclusion has not been measured in the human thalamus. These results propose regional SRRM4 supply as a testable determinant of CPEB4 microexon splicing and identify the measurements needed to test it: microexon inclusion and SRRM4, PTBP1 and PTBP2 protein in thalamic nuclei and cingulate cortex.

title: Hepatic microRNA expression profiling in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) fed an insect meal-based diet and implications for the regulation of lipid metabolism and detoxification pathways.
abstract: The use of insect meals as sustainable alternatives to fishmeal is rapidly expanding in aquaculture, yet the molecular and epigenetic responses they elicit remain poorly understood. This study investigated the hepatic microRNA (miRNA) landscape of rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) fed diets containing 3% and 20% Hermetia illucens (HI) full-fat meal. Small RNA sequencing was performed to identify differentially expressed miRNAs and their predicted functional implications. qPCR confirmed the expression patterns of selected miRNAs and revealed corresponding changes in the expression of computationally predicted target genes, including nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NFE2L2), cytochrome P450 1 A (CYP1A), ATP-binding cassette sub-family A1 (ABCA1), serine/threonine kinase 3 (AKT3) and Sterol Regulatory Element-Binding Protein 2 (SREBP2), that were consistent with putative miRNA-mRNA associations. KEGG and Reactome analyses revealed the modulation of pathways related to lipid metabolism, oxidative stress, detoxification and intracellular trafficking. The LOW diet (3% HI) induced a broad enrichment of metabolic pathways, suggesting a physiological adaptation to a moderate inclusion of insect meal. Conversely, the HIGH diet (20% HI) was characterized by the potential regulation of extracellular matrix remodeling, glycosaminoglycan metabolism and cytoskeletal regulation, indicative of a more complex tissue organization. These findings provide novel mechanistic insights into the miRNA-mediated regulatory networks underlying the hepatic adaptation of rainbow trout to insect-based diets, contributing to a better understanding of the molecular responses elicited by sustainable feed ingredients.
